cim_eredeti: How to Set Up a Team of AI Agents for Your Small Business With Symphony
szoveg_eredeti:
If you purchase through a link on our site, we may earn a commission.

A small business is often pulled between many tasks at once. There’s an even greater pull during sales periods, as you need to create the right offer, market it, and build your site’s pages. From there, you have to follow up on the influx of inquiries. Some of this inevitably doesn’t happen to your satisfaction. However, as this Symphony tutorial will show you, the outcome can change.

👉 Read the full Symphony review on the WP Mayor blog.

This tutorial is a follow-on from my Symphony review and walks through a real-world example of how you’d use Symphony for a sales page.

The short overview of Symphony is: you chat with Maestro about your business and goals. It then builds a team of AI agents and delegates the work. Each agent owns a specific area, such as finance, design, or research.

I’m going to run through a typical small business sale with prompt examples, approval settings, agent assignments, and more. To follow along, you need Symphony, the free version of Jetpack, a Gmail account, and Google Calendar access.

After the initial setup process, you chat with Maestro using the toolbar at the bottom of the page. Or, you can head to the Home screen to find some inspiration for your goals:

During the onboarding, Maestro gave me an initial plan, but I want to run a sale. Here’s an example prompt I used:

Hollowfield Pottery is a one-person pottery studio. For Black Friday, I want to sell more gift vouchers between November 27 and 30 without discounting more than 20%. This needs to be through my WordPress website only. Help me plan it.

The more context you give this initial prompt, the better the plan and team Maestro builds. This plan needs your input and confirmation.

In my case, I next needed to make some decisions about the sale’s specifics. Regardless, Maestro or the AI agents take no action until you approve.

Once you confirm the plan, Maestro builds the team, delegates to specialist agents, then comes to you for sign-off. Your job is to make sure the team fits your goals and needs. My advice is to check the team over once it’s ready, much like you would with a human team.

For this sale, I have agents ready to roll. Two are important for this part of the process:

The job description for each agent is the best way to find out how it will support the task. You can find this through clicking one of the names on the Agents screen.

If something needs a change, the way to do so is to bring it to the attention of Maestro. There’s no settings panel for these kinds of changes, so everything requires a conversation.

You might also see some Routines at this stage, depending on your project and goals. For example, Maestro might recommend a daily briefing or team meeting. You can switch these on or off using the toggles within the Routines screen within your project’s workspace, so only activate the ones you need.

Maestro and your AI agents can only work and act on the tools you connect. You’re welcome to ask Maestro directly to help set up any connections, but there’s also the Settings > Connectors and MCPs page:

I’m connecting to some Google tools, so each one needs approval. Gmail in particular requires full access to read, send, and organize email. If you also want to connect your email but use a shared inbox, you may want to connect to a separate address.

Next is connecting your WordPress website. I’m doing it through the My Jetpack > Features > Jetpack AI screen within the plugin. Here, choose the MCP and Connectors tab, then toggle the External AI agent access option on:

I also had to set these same switches on my WordPress.com account, then click a connector card for WordPress in Maestro.

With connections in place, you can set up checks for quality and accuracy. Jetpack has its own activity log specifically for AI agent actions. My view is that you should check it after every step, especially if it’s the first time you run it.

Another check you can run often is to ask questions about your site to confirm the connection works. For example:

Which pages are on my site and what does the contact page ask visitors for?

The response tells you whether you need to make changes.

The next few steps are all about the actual work of setting up a sales offer and building the content. I’m starting with a prompt:

Plan our Black Friday gift voucher offer. There will be 20% off vouchers bought between November 27-30, and a free mug-painting session for anyone who buys two vouchers.

Write the offer terms, then draft a sale page on my WordPress site with a headline, the offer, the terms, and a link to the contact form. Keep the page as a draft for now.

Once you confirm the prompt and task, the agents will get to work. I had to answer some further questions and make a couple of changes to the original voucher offer, which is typical.

To check the draft sales page, open it up in the Site Editor using the link Maestro gives you.

I’d recommend publishing the page yourself if everything looks okay. I’d probably also make small changes myself, but go back to your agents to make larger, sweeping changes.

With an offer ready to promote and a sales page, you can begin to market the offer through social media and your newsletter. Here’s an example prompt:

Write an email about the Black Friday gift voucher offer, suitable for our past customers subscribed to the newsletter. Also write three Instagram and Facebook posts with an open-sourced image for each. Use a warm, plain tone. Don’t send or post anything until I approve it.

You then need to check over this draft email and three social posts. It’s likely that these will need edits, but again, I’d leave bigger changes to the agents. You can help them along through adding example files and screenshots using the Plus icon in the chat toolbar.

You can ask for the drafts inline (as I did), in a separate file, or another suitable format. Maestro will even save the email to your Gmail drafts if you ask:

If you’re struggling to find a connection on the Settings > Connectors and MCPs screen, Maestro can find it.

For instance, I couldn’t see an Instagram connector at first, but still got a card for it in a fresh chat window.

During a busy sales period, tasks such as following up with all the inquiries, bookings, quotes, and other incoming messages can fall by the wayside. You can ask Maestro to put together a solution for this. Here’s an example prompt:

Check my contact form responses every morning. Draft a reply to each new inquiry, but don’t send it.

Check for any sent emails. Set a follow up after two days if there’s no answer, and suggest times from my calendar for anyone who wants to book. Ask me before you send anything.

As with the newsletter copy, Maestro drafts a response to each of the inquiries in my inbox.

I can edit things further or send it back to Maestro for changes. This is also set up as a Routine. If I want to run it early, I just have to ask.

As an aside, processes such as this need a greater ‘credit budget‘ to accommodate them. In my review, I recommended an annual Pro plan as you get a healthy number of credits, among other benefits.

The day after your tasks run is as important as the day itself. This is when you check for responses, look at analytics, and see how your campaign is going.

Before you log off for the evening and leave the agents to work overnight, check all your tasks over. Also, look for your daily team briefing settings and toggle this on. When you receive it, take a look at what it includes as yours might be different from mine.

In the Home section, you can see the outcome of all agent tasks. It also lets you approve any waiting actions. If you’re working with Symphony using the iOS and Android apps, you get approval notifications direct to your phone.
